title: El Cantante
full_review:
"The bigger he was as an artist, the deeper he sank as a human being," declares Nilda Georgina Roman (Jennifer Lopez), widow of groundbreaking salsa star Hector Lavoe.

That statement pretty accurately sums up the dramatic arc of "El Cantante" (Picturehouse), a biography tracing the Puerto Rican singer's musical rise to fame and then downward spiral. He's played most persuasively by Lopez's real-life husband -- and salsa singer himself -- Marc Anthony. Though Hector's musical successes are well limned, so are the damaging drug addictions and other destructive behavior (mainly substance abuse) that would lead to his death from AIDS at 46.

The film charts Hector from his origins in Puerto Rico, where his father threatened to disown him if he went to the States; his meeting with wild, vulgar clubgoer Nilda (nicknamed Puchi); and the fractious marriage that followed, marked by raging fights, accusations of infidelity on both sides and the death of their son in an accidental shooting.

Hector's habitual tardiness and unreliability eventually cause a rift with bandleader Willie Colon (John Ortiz), who partnered with Hector on his biggest hits.

The stars are fine. Anthony delivers the vocal goods on this occasion, offering a credible dramatic performance, too. A tough-talking Lopez shows considerably more range than ever before, and manages to convey her genuine love for Hector, beneath Puchi's often unlikable vulgarity. She, too, was a drug user, though the film presents her as the more stable of the pair.

It is a black-and-white re-creation of a 2002 interview with Puchi looking back on her life with Hector that frames the film, which superficially has something of the flavor of "Lenny," Bob Fosse's classic film about another wretched life, that of comedian Lenny Bruce.

Director Leon Ichaso, who co-wrote the script with David Darmstaedter and Todd Anthony Bello, re-creates the era convincingly in this over-the-decades saga (from the 1960s onward), and there's a bountiful musical earful throughout for fans of that music.

But, it must be said, the couple's endless bickering and the nonstop barrage of expletives are repetitious -- stretches of dialogue seem comprised of little more than a volleying of the f-word -- and ultimately wearying.

The film contains pervasive rough language, drug and alcohol abuse, attempted suicide, premarital situations, some nongraphic sexual encounters, innuendo, implied adultery and a brief suggestion of sexual kinkiness, and some skimpy costuming. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
